newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich wins easily, now faces harder tasks.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich wins easily, now faces harder tasks.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich easily trounced his wealthy Democratic opponent in Tuesday's election but now faces the harder tasks of defending himself in an expanded ethics investigation and unifying his party.

The Georgia Republican will preside over a House Republican majority that is smaller and which owes little to the revolutionary political agenda he pushed in the last congressional session. Still, it is the first back-to-back victory for Republicans since 1928.
And, with Republican control of the Senate, the election put President Clinton on the defensive for his second term.
At a news conference in Georgia on Wednesday, Gingrich said his party will not pick symbolic fights when the new Congress gets underway in January.

He urged Democrats to join with them "to find common ground." In post-election news conferences, Gingrich and other party leaders spoke of willingness to listen to President Clinton's views and consider his agenda in January.

As House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas told ABC television, there would be more cooperation with the White House. "I think we'll work better. First of all, we've all learned a great deal," he said.

Democrats fell short of picking up 19 seats to take control but cut the Republican majority by about half with several races still undecided. Before the election, the lineup was 235-197, with one independent and two vacancies.

The election leaves Gingrich with a mixed outcome. He remains extremely popular with the Republican faithful but has a reduced power base within his own House. And yet, the 73 freshmen he worked to see elected in 1994 fared well. No more than 15 lost; two did not run and one went to the Senate.

While Democrats used Gingrich's record as a whip against Republican candidates, and some in his party distanced themselves from Gingrich, the speaker proved popular with Republican faithful across the country. He made frequent trips to Republican fundraisers in many states, attending even if the local candidates did not.

"When all is said and done, the speaker will have raised for our committee or our candidates in excess of $100 million this cycle," National Republican Congressional Committee chairman Representative Bill Paxon of New York told reporters on Wednesday.
Nationally, polls showed voters blamed Republicans for the two highly unpopular government shutdowns last winter.

In 1994, Republicans ran on the ten-point Contract with America agenda put forth by Gingrich and House Republicans to win what they said was a mandate for smaller government and major reforms in the way Congress was run.

For Gingrich, who managed in the last session to consolidate much of the power over appointments to House committees in his office, attention will be diverted by pressures of an expanded investigation into whether his tax-exempt foundation used funds improperly to help freshmen Republicans win House seats in 1994.

Criticism about the slow pace of the investigation proved damaging for Connecticut Republican Nancy Johnson, head of the bipartisan ethics committee, who teetered on the edge of defeat when votes were being counted Wednesday. Both Johnson and Democrat Charlotte Koskoff were said to be leading at points during the day.
